Wine department

Canelones

The department of Canelones, to the north and east of Montevideo, holds most of Uruguay’s vineyards. On clay soils and under the influence of the Río de la Plata and the Atlantic, it is the heartland of Uruguayan Tannat and home to many historic family wineries.

History

Viticulture in Canelones is linked to European immigration in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Families of Italian, Spanish, Basque and French origin settled on the smallholdings near Montevideo, planted vines and created small wineries that sold their wine in the capital. Many of today’s well-known wineries, such as Pizzorno, Pisano and Juanicó, date from that period or are run by descendants of those immigrants. The proximity of the large Montevideo market explains why Canelones became the country’s leading production area, a position it still holds. From the 1980s, the conversion of vineyards to selected clones of Tannat and other European varieties, together with the modernisation of wineries, transformed the quality of its wines.

Climate

The climate is temperate and humid, with abundant rainfall spread throughout the year. The influence of the Río de la Plata estuary and the Atlantic Ocean is constant: breezes moderate summer heat and cool nights help preserve acidity. Rain during ripening and humidity are the main challenge, since they favour fungal diseases; growers therefore pay close attention to air flow around the bunches through training systems and canopy management. The wines tend to have moderate alcohol and marked acidity.

Soils

Clay and silty clay soils predominate, deep and fertile, often with a dense clay layer at depth that retains water. In some areas there is calcium carbonate. The relief is gentle, with low rolling hills, and the aspect and drainage of each plot affect vine vigour and grape quality. The clays give structure to the reds, especially Tannat.

Areas

Vineyards are spread across many localities in the department, such as Las Piedras, Progreso, Juanicó, Canelón Chico, Los Cerrillos, Las Violetas, Sauce and Santa Lucía, as well as the neighbouring areas of the department of Montevideo, such as Melilla, with which they form a single winegrowing core. Uruguay has no appellation system comparable to Europe’s, so wineries state the area or vineyard of origin on the label.

Varieties and styles

Tannat is the most planted variety and the one that defines the region, giving deeply coloured reds with firm tannins and black fruit, made both in a young style and with barrel ageing, and often blended with Merlot, Cabernet Franc or Cabernet Sauvignon to soften its structure. Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Syrah are also grown. Among whites, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and, increasingly, Albariño stand out. Rosés, sparkling wines and some sweet Tannat wines are also made.

Country
Uruguay
Climate
Temperate and humid, with year-round rainfall and strong influence from the Río de la Plata and the Atlantic.
Soils
Clay and silty clay, deep, with dense clay layers at depth.
Styles
Tannat reds, varietal or blended, fresh whites, rosés and sparkling wines.
Grapes
Tannat, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Syrah (Shiraz), Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Albariño
